dossiers.inflation-taux.hook: Has your grocery bill gone up 20% in just a few years? From American gold sending prices haywire in the 16th century to the wheelbarrows of banknotes in 1923, from the Volcker shock to the ECB in 2022, here is the history and mechanics of inflation, along with the debates that still divide economists.
dossiers.inflation-taux.tldr.0: Inflation is a general and lasting rise in prices: the same banknote buys less. In 2022, it topped 5% in France, a level not seen since the mid-1980s [1].
dossiers.inflation-taux.tldr.1: The idea that a flood of money drives prices up dates back at least to 1568, when Jean Bodin explained rising prices in Europe by the gold and silver arriving from the Americas [3].
dossiers.inflation-taux.tldr.2: When it spirals out of control, it destroys everything: in November 1923, one dollar was worth 4,200 billion German marks [4]; in November 2008, prices in Zimbabwe reportedly rose by 79.6 billion percent in a single month [5].
dossiers.inflation-taux.tldr.3: To slow it down, central banks raise their interest rates. In the United States, Paul Volcker pushed the Fed's rate up to 20% around 1980-1981, at the cost of 10.8% unemployment [6]. The ECB went from negative rates to 4% between 2022 and 2023 [2][10].
dossiers.inflation-taux.tldr.4: In 2022-2023, corporate profits accounted for about 45% of the rise in prices in the euro area, and import prices (energy) for about 40%, according to the IMF [11].
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.0.title: Where does inflation come from?
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.0.parag: ==Inflation== is a general and lasting rise in prices. “General”: not just the price of tomatoes or petrol, but prices as a whole. “Lasting”: not a one-week spike. When inflation is 5%, a basket that cost 100 euros costs 105 a year later; with the same salary, you buy less.

Economists distinguish three main causes. ==Cost-push inflation==: energy, raw materials or wages go up, and companies pass the increase on to their prices. ==Demand-pull inflation==: people want to buy more than the economy can produce, and prices climb. ==Monetary inflation==: too much money in circulation compared with the goods available.

Add to this a psychological ingredient: ==expectations==. If everyone expects 10% inflation, employees ask for a 10% raise, companies raise their prices by 10% as a precaution, and the forecast fulfils itself. That is why central banks care so much about their credibility: if people believe they will bring inflation back to 2%, half the job is done.

In 2021-2022, several causes piled up: the post-Covid recovery made demand soar, supply chains were disrupted (stuck containers, chip shortages), and then the war in Ukraine sent gas, oil and grain prices through the roof. The result: 5.2% inflation in France in 2022 and 4.9% in 2023 [1].
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.1.title: How it is measured
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.1.parag: In France, inflation is measured by Insee, the national statistics institute, using the ==consumer price index== (CPI) [1]. Every month, field surveyors and checkout data record the prices of thousands of goods and services across the country: food, rent, energy, clothing, transport, hairdressers, insurance…

Each product is weighted according to its share of the average household budget: energy or rent count more than matches. The cost of this “basket” is then compared from one month or one year to the next.

Hence a frequent misunderstanding between ==measured inflation and perceived inflation==. The basket is that of an average household; a young person renting in a city, a retiree heating with oil or a rural household driving 50 km a day do not have the same one. And people mostly notice the prices of frequent purchases (bread, petrol), much less those that fall (televisions, phones of equal performance).

Central banks also look at ==core inflation==, which strips out the most volatile prices (energy, fresh food). It shows whether the rise is taking hold across the whole economy or comes from a temporary shock.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.1.examp: If you spend 40% of your budget on rent, 20% on groceries and 10% on transport, and groceries go up 10%, your “groceries” inflation weighs 20% × 10% = 2 points in your personal inflation. If your rent is frozen, you may experience lower inflation than average; if you fill up your tank every day during an oil shock, much higher.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.2.title: 1568: American gold and the first explanation
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.2.parag: In the 16th century, Europe went through what historians call the ==“price revolution”==: after centuries of relative stability, prices rose steadily for decades. Nobody understood why.

In France, a royal adviser, Jean de Malestroit, blamed coin clipping and the falling metal content of coins. In 1568, the jurist ==Jean Bodin== answered him in a now-famous essay: the real cause, he said, was ==the flood of gold and silver arriving from the New World== through Spain [3]. The more precious metal there is, the less each gram is worth, so the more of it you need to buy the same thing.

This is one of the first statements of what would later be called the ==quantity theory of money==: if the quantity of money grows faster than the quantity of goods, prices rise [3]. Historians point out that Bodin was not quite the first: in Salamanca, the theologian Martín de Azpilcueta had made the same connection about a dozen years earlier [3].

Four centuries later, the economist Milton Friedman took up the idea in a famous phrase: “inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon” (see our course on the major schools of economic thought). Keynesians would reply that costs and demand matter too. The debate is not settled.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.3.title: When money becomes worthless: 1923 and 2008
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.3.parag: Economists speak of ==hyperinflation== when prices rise by more than 50% a month. The most famous example is Germany in 1923. To pay for its spending and the reparations from the First World War, the state ran the printing presses. In November 1923, ==one dollar was worth about 4,200 billion marks== [4]. A loaf of bread that cost about 160 marks at the end of 1922 cost about 200 billion by the end of 1923 [4].

Workers were paid twice a day and rushed to spend their wages before they melted away; children played with bundles of banknotes, and people papered walls with them. On 15 November 1923, a new currency, the ==Rentenmark==, replaced the old mark: 1 Rentenmark for 1,000 billion marks [4]. The middle classes, whose savings had been wiped out, kept a lasting distrust, which partly explains Germany's attachment to a stable currency.

More recently, ==Zimbabwe== broke every record. As the state no longer published reliable figures, the economist Steve Hanke of Johns Hopkins University estimated that by mid-November 2008, prices were rising by ==79.6 billion percent a month== [5], roughly doubling every day. The country eventually abandoned its own currency in favour of the US dollar and other currencies.

These episodes all have one thing in common: ==a state that finances its spending by creating money==, often after a war, a collapse in production or a political crisis. That is why most countries have made their central bank independent of the government.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.3.plain: The state can no longer pay its expenses with taxes, so it has banknotes printed.
There are more banknotes for the same amount of bread: the price of bread goes up.
Seeing prices rise, people spend their money as fast as possible before it loses its value: demand spirals.
Prices rise even faster, and the state prints even more to keep up: in 1923, one dollar ends up being worth 4,200 billion marks [4].
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.4.title: The 1970s and the Volcker shock
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.4.parag: In the 1970s, rich countries discovered ==stagflation==: high inflation and unemployment at the same time, something the theories of the day considered almost impossible. The oil shocks of 1973 and 1979 sent energy prices soaring, and wages indexed to prices kept the increase going.

In August 1979, Paul Volcker became head of the US Federal Reserve. On 6 October 1979, he announced a change of course: the Fed would strictly control the quantity of money, even if it meant letting rates climb [6]. The policy rate reached ==a record 20% around 1980-1981== [6].

The cure was brutal. Loans became prohibitively expensive, farmers blockaded Washington with their tractors, and companies went bankrupt. ==Unemployment reached 10.8% at the end of 1982== [6]. But inflation fell: it dropped to 6.1% in early 1982 [6], then stayed moderate for decades.

The “Volcker shock” remains the benchmark for central bankers: it shows that entrenched inflation can be beaten, but at a high cost, especially when action comes late. This is one of the reasons why the Fed and the ECB raised their rates so quickly in 2022.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.5.title: France in 1982: freezing prices, then de-indexing
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.5.parag: In France too, inflation exceeded 13% in 1980 and 1981. After the 1981 stimulus (see our IS-LM course), the government changed course. In ==June 1982==, on the initiative of Finance Minister Jacques Delors, it devalued the franc and ==froze prices and wages for four months== [7].

Then came the decisive measure: the ==de-indexation of wages==. Until then, many wages automatically followed rising prices, which kept a loop going: prices go up, so wages go up, so costs go up, so prices go up. By no longer aligning wage increases with past inflation and setting them instead on target inflation, the state broke the loop [7].

The result was spectacular: inflation fell from ==12% in 1982 to 3.1% in 1988== [7]. The price paid is debated: slower growth in employees' purchasing power and rising unemployment in the following years.

This memory explains why, in 2022-2023, the debate on wage indexation was so heated: should purchasing power be protected through indexation, at the risk of restarting the wage-price loop? Most countries chose targeted support and minimum wage increases rather than general indexation.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.6.title: Why 2%, and not 0%?
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.6.parag: In the euro area, the European Central Bank (ECB) watches over prices. Its target: inflation of 2% a year over the medium term [2]. Not too much (people get poorer), not too little (the economy dozes off).

This figure comes from a small country. ==New Zealand== was the first country to officially give its central bank a numerical inflation target: the 1989 law came into force on 1 February 1990 [9]. The target was first a range of 3 to 5%, then 0 to 2% [9]. The success of the experiment set an example: Canada, the United Kingdom, Sweden and then most central banks adopted a target close to 2%.

Why not zero? First, price indices tend to slightly overestimate inflation (products improve without the price fully reflecting it). Second, ==deflation (falling prices) is dangerous==: if prices fall, people put off their purchases, waiting for them to fall further; companies sell less and lay off staff, and debt becomes harder to repay. Japan was caught in this trap for years.

Finally, a little inflation gives central banks room to manoeuvre: with 2% inflation, interest rates are normally higher, so they can be cut further in a crisis. Some economists even argue for a 3% target; others think that would mean giving up hard-won credibility.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.7.title: The role of the central bank
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.7.parag: Its main tool is its ==policy rates==: the price at which banks borrow from it or deposit their money with it. These rates then feed through to all the loans in the economy.

For years, the ECB's problem was not inflation that was too high, but too low. In ==June 2014==, it did something rare: it took its deposit rate ==below zero, to −0.10%== [10]. Banks paid to leave their money at the ECB, which was meant to push them to lend. The rate went as low as −0.50% in 2019 [2].

Then everything reversed. On ==21 July 2022==, the ECB raised its rates for the first time in eleven years, by 0.5 points [2]. Ten consecutive increases followed: in ==September 2023, the deposit rate reached 4%==, the fastest rise in its history [2]. Cuts only resumed in June 2024.

The ECB also has other tools: buying or selling bonds (known as “quantitative easing” or its reverse) and, above all, ==words==: by explaining what it intends to do, it steers expectations. In 2012, at the height of the euro crisis, its president Mario Draghi promised to do “whatever it takes” to save the euro; those three words were enough to calm the markets.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.8.title: Why raising rates calms prices
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.8.parag: When rates go up, mortgages, car loans and business loans become more expensive. Households and companies borrow and spend less, demand slows, and so do prices.

Rates also work through other channels. ==Savings== earn more, which encourages people to spend less. ==The currency== strengthens, because capital flows in seeking better returns: imported goods become cheaper. And ==expectations== calm down, if people believe the central bank will see it through.

The downside: less investment, a housing market that seizes up, governments paying more on their debt, and a risk of slowing the economy too sharply. It is a delicate balance, a bit like braking a car without stalling it. And the effects take time to arrive: it is often estimated that a rate rise takes one to two years to have its full effect on prices.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.8.plain: rising rates, all the way to your wallet
The ECB raises its policy rate (July 2022, then again and again up to 4% in September 2023) [2].
Banks borrow at a higher cost and raise the rates on their mortgages, car loans and business loans.
Households buy fewer homes and cars, companies postpone their investments: demand slows.
Companies find it harder to raise their prices: inflation falls, from 5.2% in 2022 to 2% in 2024 in France [1].
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.9.title: 2022: who is to blame? Wages, profits or energy
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.9.parag: During the 2022 surge, one question divided economists and policymakers: what is driving prices up? ==Wages== (the “wage-price spiral”), imported ==energy==, or company ==profits==?

In June 2023, three IMF economists published a breakdown of the rise in prices in the euro area. Between early 2022 and early 2023, ==corporate profits accounted for about 45% of the increase, import prices for about 40%==, and wages far less [11]. In other words, many companies raised their prices by more than their costs.

The term ==“profitflation”== (or “greedflation”) became popular. But the authors themselves are cautious: a rise in profits in euros does not necessarily mean a rise in profitability, and some companies were making up for losses [11]. They also expected wages to catch up with prices in 2023-2024, and profits would then have to absorb these increases for inflation to recede [11].

This debate shows that the same statistic can serve opposing narratives. Above all, remember that ==inflation is a battle over how the pie is shared==: when prices rise, everyone (employees, companies, governments, energy-exporting countries) tries not to be the one who pays.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.10.para: There is a discreet way to raise prices: ==reduce the quantity while keeping the same price==. The packet of biscuits goes from 200 to 180 grams, the bottle from 1.5 to 1.25 litres, and the label does not change. This is ==“shrinkflation”== (in French, « réduflation »).

The price index takes these changes into account, because it tracks the price per kilo or per litre. But customers often do not notice. In response to complaints, France issued a decree in 2024: since ==1 July 2024==, shops must flag for two months any products whose quantity has decreased and whose price per kilo or per litre has risen [12].

Its effectiveness remains limited: a few months later, a check by the consumer association UFC-Que Choisir found no labelling at all in 95% of the shops visited [12]. The useful habit is still to look at the ==price per kilo or per litre==, which must be displayed on the shelf label.
dossiers.inflation-taux.sections.11.para: Inflation does not make everyone poorer in the same way. ==Fixed-rate borrowers gain==: their monthly payment stays the same, while their salary eventually rises. A mortgage taken out at 1% in 2021 became much lighter after 10% cumulative inflation.

==Savers lose== if their money earns less than inflation: a savings account at 3% with 5% inflation loses 2% of purchasing power a year. ==Employees and retirees== lose as long as their income does not keep up with prices. ==Low-income households== are often the hardest hit, because food and energy, which rose the most in 2022, weigh more heavily in their budget.

==The state== is in an ambiguous position: inflation swells its revenue (VAT follows prices) and lightens the relative weight of its old debt, but it raises the rates at which it borrows and the cost of support measures. ==Companies== that can raise their prices do fine; those that cannot suffer.

That is why inflation is as much a political issue as an economic one: behind an average figure lie transfers of wealth between generations, between savers and borrowers, between employees and companies.
dossiers.inflation-taux.forMe: When inflation rises, look at what earns less than it does (your current account, some savings accounts) and what keeps up with prices. Compare products by the price per kilo, not the price per packet. And if you ever borrow at a fixed rate, remember that moderate inflation lightens your debt over the years.

dossiers.ecoles-economiques.tldr.4: Economics did not stop at the great quarrels over the state and the market: since 2000, Nobel prizes have rewarded those who show that we are not so rational (Kahneman in 2002, Thaler in 2017) [10][12], that communities manage shared resources very well without the state or the market (Ostrom, the first woman laureate, in 2009) [11], and that policies can be tested by random assignment, as in medicine (Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer in 2019) [13].
dossiers.ecoles-economiques.sections.9.p: Before becoming textbook names, Keynes and Hayek were flesh-and-blood opponents. In 1931, the London School of Economics invited the young Austrian ==Friedrich Hayek== to London, partly to counter the influence of Keynes, who was based in Cambridge. What followed was an exchange of critiques and replies in the journals of rare intensity.

The heart of the disagreement is simple to sum up. For ==Keynes==, the crisis comes from a lack of spending: the economy must be stimulated. For ==Hayek==, the crisis is the hangover from an artificial boom, fuelled by credit that was too cheap and led to investment in bad projects: stimulating means prolonging the illness; the economy must be allowed to purge itself.

In the 1930s, Keynes won the battle of ideas, and his 1936 “General Theory” dominated the post-war period. But Hayek later got his revenge: awarded the Nobel prize in 1974, the very year of stagflation [9], he inspired Margaret Thatcher and the liberals of the 1980s. After the 2008 crisis, the debate came back almost word for word: stimulate or let the economy purge?
This duel shows that ==schools of thought are not just theories: they are different answers to the same question==, “what should be done when everything collapses?”.
The behaviourists: we are not so rational

Almost all the schools seen so far assume that people calculate their interest well. In the 1970s, two Israeli psychologists, ==Daniel Kahneman== and Amos Tversky, showed through experiments that we make mistakes in ==predictable== ways: we fear a loss more than we value a gain of the same size, we let ourselves be influenced by the first number we hear, and we favour the present over the future more than is reasonable.

In ==2002==, Kahneman received the Nobel prize in economics for bringing these findings from psychology into economics, particularly on decision-making under uncertainty [10]. A psychologist receiving the economics prize: a sign that the discipline was opening up.

The American economist ==Richard Thaler== extended this work. He popularised the idea of the ==“nudge”==: without banning or forcing anything, you can help people make better choices by changing the way the options are presented. A famous example: automatically enrolling employees in a retirement savings plan, while leaving them free to opt out, sharply increases savings. Thaler received the Nobel prize in ==2017== [12].

This school does not replace the others, but it corrects them: it explains stock market bubbles, excessive debt, and why people fail to claim benefits they are entitled to. It also has its critics: ==who decides what the “right” choice is, and how far can the state steer us?==
the power of the default option
A company offers a retirement savings plan: to join, you have to fill in a form. Many employees put it off.
The same company enrols everyone automatically, with the option to leave in one click.
Almost nobody opts out: the inertia that used to work against saving now works for it.
Nobody was forced, but the outcome changes a lot: that is Thaler's idea of the “nudge” [12].
Elinor Ostrom: neither the state nor the market

In 1968, the biologist Garrett Hardin published a famous article, “The Tragedy of the Commons”: when a resource is shared (a pasture, a fishing ground), everyone has an interest in exploiting it as much as possible before the others, and it ends up destroyed. The classic solutions: ==privatise== it (the market) or have it managed by ==the state==.

The American political scientist ==Elinor Ostrom== went to see for herself in the field. Swiss pastures, irrigation systems in Nepal, fisheries in Turkey, forests in Japan: she found that ==communities manage their shared resources very well for centuries==, with their own rules, their own monitoring and their own sanctions, without privatisation or a central state.

She drew principles from this: clear boundaries, rules adapted to the place, users who take part in decisions, monitoring by the community, graduated sanctions. In ==2009==, she became ==the first woman to receive the Nobel prize in economics== [11].

Her work is now widely used to think about the great modern “commons”: the climate, the oceans, water, and even free software and Wikipedia. It challenges the idea that there are only two options, the market or the state.
The experimenters: testing economics like a medicine

For a long time, economics reasoned mainly from models and past statistics. From the 1990s onwards, a new generation decided to ==test policies by random assignment==, the way a medicine is tested: one group receives the support, another does not, and the results are compared.

The leading figures of this movement are ==Abhijit Banerjee==, ==Esther Duflo== (French, trained at the École normale supérieure) and ==Michael Kremer==. In India, Kenya and elsewhere, they test what really works against poverty: should mosquito nets be handed out free or sold? Should more teachers be added, or should pupils be grouped by level? Should children be dewormed so that they attend school more?

In ==2019==, all three received the Nobel prize for their “experimental approach to alleviating global poverty” [13]. At 46, Esther Duflo was then the youngest laureate and the second woman in the history of the prize [13].

This is also the method Raj Chetty used for Moving to Opportunity (see our course on social mobility). Its strength: precise answers. Its limit: what works in a Kenyan village does not necessarily work elsewhere, and ==you cannot randomly assign a monetary policy or a trade war==. The major schools therefore keep their role for the big questions.
==1776==: Adam Smith, “The Wealth of Nations” [1]. ==1817==: Ricardo, comparative advantage. ==1848==: Marx and Engels, “The Communist Manifesto”. ==1870s==: Walras, Jevons and Menger, the marginalist revolution [2].

==1931==: the Keynes-Hayek duel begins. ==1936==: Keynes, “General Theory” [3]. ==1937==: Hicks invents the IS-LM model. ==1969==: first Nobel prize in economics. ==1970==: Samuelson, Nobel prize [4]. ==1974==: Hayek, Nobel prize, in the midst of stagflation [9]. ==1976==: Friedman, Nobel prize [5].

==1995==: Lucas, Nobel prize for rational expectations [6]. ==2001==: Akerlof, Spence and Stiglitz, imperfect information [8]. ==2002==: Kahneman, psychology enters economics [10]. ==2009==: Ostrom, first woman laureate [11]. ==2017==: Thaler, the “nudge” [12]. ==2019==: Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer, experiments against poverty [13].
The common thread: ==economics advances through crises and controversies==, and each generation corrects the lenses of the one before.
